clues.text: In chapter five of Utilitarianism, J.S. Mill examined many definitions of this concept.
Robert Nozick argues that requirements for this concept are not satisfied by end-result and pattern principles in Anarchy, State, and Utopia, while Hume defined it as an artificial virtue.
The distinction between Aristotlean and Humean conceptions of this attribute is discussed in a 1988 text asking "whose" this thing and "which rationality" by Alasdair MacIntyre.

One theorist used reflective equilibrium to refine the understanding of it, and his work states that a foundation in the “original position” and the difference principle are necessary to this concept.

This attribute is mentioned in the title of an earlier text that advocates a "greatest equal liberty principle" and argues for a "distributive" version of this attribute by positing an "original position" behind a "veil of ignorance."
The “original position” thought experiment, which places one behind a “veil of ignorance,” is posited in a “Theory” of this concept by John Rawls.
John Rawls equated this concept with fairness in a work titled A Theory of this, and Plato argued against a description of this concept as “the advantage of the stronger” in The Republic.
Hobbes claimed that this concept does not exist in the state of nature.
John Rawls wrote A Theory of what desirable attribute which should be produced by courts in the legal system?

clues.text: A book in this movement comparing it to the most important “cultural current” of the century, Freudianism, was written by Shulamith Firestone.
A text from this movement declares that the “problem that has no name” is people thinking, “Is this all?”
A book about this movement's theory "from margin to center" was written by bell hooks.
Within this movement, Kimberlé Crenshaw created a framework in which subordination is heightened from overlapping identities.
A book from this movement opens with the section “Facts and Myths.”
William Godwin wrote the “memoirs” of an early member of this movement who wrote a “vindication” in response to Charles Talleyrand.
The section “Lived Experiences” from that book in this movement contains the quote “One is not born, but rather becomes” a certain type of person.
This movement is currently in its “third wave” in the US; its second wave was pioneered by the founder of NOW, Betty Friedan.
Name this movement whose “second wave” included Simone de Beauvoir, who wrote The Second Sex.
Intersectionality is central to what movements its third wave?
In one work, this man criticized the progress resulting from art and science as empowering governments and undermining friendship in Discourse on the Arts and Sciences.

This man argued that the amour propre has led to a decrease in compassion in civil society in a work originally paired with his essay positing that communication became less emotional and more rational as humans moved to colder climates, Essay on the Origin of Languages.
A book by this thinker introduced a dilemma in which two agents face a choice between hunting hares alone or stags together.
This thinker’s last work was the autobiographical Reveries of a Solitary Walker, and a previous autobiography chronicled a love affair with Madame de Warens.
This man held that amour propre should restrain self-interest.

This author of Discourse on Inequality advises that the abstractions inherent in religious issues should be reserved until late childhood in a work describing the hands-off instruction and maturation of the titular boy.
This thinker opened one book by declaring, “everything degenerates in the hands of man;” that work contains the controversial “Profession of Faith of the Savoyard Vicar” passage.
This author of Essay on the Origin of Languages and Discourse on Inequality wrote a treatise on education called Emile.
He was an early supporter of direct democracy, or "popular sovereignty".
Name this man who discussed education in Emile, the Swiss Enlightenment author of The Social Contract.
